name: LakeSoul
summary: A lakehouse table format, first built by DMetaSoul, that keeps all metadata and commits in PostgreSQL and stores primary-key tables as hash buckets with merge-on-read upserts, aimed at CDC ingestion and frequent updates.
intro: LakeSoul keeps its catalog in a PostgreSQL database instead of metadata files: tables, partitions, the list of data files in each version and every commit. A writer commits by running a two-stage protocol inside PostgreSQL transactions, which also detect conflicting writers and give readers a consistent snapshot. PostgreSQL triggers notify LakeSoul’s background services when something changes, so compaction and cleanup of expired data start on their own, and PostgreSQL roles and row-level security separate workspaces. The data files are Parquet or, since 4.0, Vortex (the default for new writes), on S3 or HDFS.

A table can have range partitions, laid out in directories like Hive, and a primary key. A primary-key table is split into a fixed number of hash buckets, each sorted by key. An upsert writes only the changed rows, or even only the changed columns, as new delta files, and readers merge the latest value for each key on the fly, much like an LSM tree, until compaction folds the deltas in. That makes many concurrent writers and column-level updates cheap, and lets joins on the key skip the shuffle. A Rust I/O layer, with Java, Python and C bindings, is shared by the Spark 3.5 and Flink 1.20 connectors (read and write), Presto and DuckDB (read), and Python clients for PyArrow, Pandas, Ray and Daft. Flink jobs can sync a whole MySQL database into LakeSoul with automatic table creation and schema changes, and read tables back as changelog streams. DMetaSoul created LakeSoul and donated it to the LF AI & Data Foundation, where it has been a sandbox project since May 2023; the current release is 4.0.0 (September 2026).
strengths: Built for updates: primary-key tables take row- and column-level upserts as small delta files, and concurrent writers to different columns don’t conflict
Metadata in PostgreSQL: commits, partition pruning and conflict checks are indexed SQL lookups; the project reports filtering a table with millions of partitions in about 50 ms
CDC built in: one Flink job syncs a whole database with new tables and DDL changes picked up automatically, exactly once, and Flink reads tables back as changelogs
Table services included: automatic compaction triggered by the metadata database, cleanup of expired and redundant data, and storage statistics
limits: Every engine and job needs a connection to the PostgreSQL metadata database, which you run, size and secure; it is the catalog for every table
Engines need LakeSoul’s own connectors: Spark 3.5 and Flink 1.20 read and write, Presto and DuckDB only read, and Spark 4 and Flink 2 are on the 2026 roadmap
Spark SQL has gaps on primary-key tables: no `INSERT INTO` (use `MERGE INTO`), `MERGE INTO` without conditional `MATCHED` clauses and only on primary-key equality, and no column type changes
A smaller ecosystem than Iceberg, Delta Lake or Hudi, and still at the foundation’s first, sandbox stage

-- primary-key tables take upserts through MERGE INTO, not INSERT INTO

story: When LakeSoul appeared, Delta Lake and Hudi kept table metadata in files next to the data. Its first README argued that this made metadata slow to parse after a table had run for a long time, that Delta Lake could only be written from a single point, and that Hudi’s merge-on-read didn’t meet its update-performance needs for primary-key data. The DMetaSoul team built LakeSoul on Spark as “a unified streaming and batch table storage solution” with metadata in Cassandra and upserts stored as delta files.

Version 2.0 in July 2022 replaced Cassandra with PostgreSQL and used its transactions for commit conflict detection, and also added snapshot reads and rollback. Version 2.1 brought Flink and whole-database CDC sync. In May 2023 DMetaSoul donated LakeSoul to the LF AI & Data Foundation as a sandbox project, and 2.3.0 that July was the first release under the foundation, with Flink SQL and global automatic compaction.

LakeSoul 3.0 in September 2025 doubled read and write speed of its Rust I/O layer compared with 2.6, added a local cache for object storage, Spark with Gluten and Presto with Velox, an Arrow Flight SQL gateway and a PyPI package. Version 4.0 followed in September 2026, with Vortex as the default file format for new writes.

choices.choice: Metadata in a database, not in files
choices.why: Its first README blamed file-based metadata for slow metadata parsing on long-running tables and for single-point writes. A database handles many concurrent commits and indexed lookups; LakeSoul started on Cassandra and moved to PostgreSQL in 2.0 to get transactions for conflict detection.

choices.choice: Upserts as delta files, merged when read
choices.why: Writing only the changed rows or columns turns updates into appends, which the project says greatly improves write throughput and concurrency; compaction merges the deltas later.

choices.choice: Hash buckets sorted by primary key
choices.why: Records with the same key always land in the same sorted bucket, so a read can merge versions without a shuffle, and joins, intersects and excepts on the key need no shuffle or sort.

choices.choice: Let the metadata database drive maintenance
choices.why: Compaction, cleanup and statistics services listen to change notifications from PostgreSQL, so they run cluster-wide without configuring each table, which 2.3 introduced to cut the cost of keeping many tables fast.
